content: Oli Freke is a musician and journalist whose works have appeared in Sound on Sound, The Quietus, and Mixmag. This has included using math to explore the melodic potential of the Western 12-tone scale and deep dives on effects plug-ins. He’s even written a book tracing the evolution of the synthesizer from 1963 through 1995, charting the change from analog to digital and back.  His new project is Beat Gems, a coffee-table visual history of drum machines from publisher Bjooks. Like other Bjooks titles, Beat Gems is loaded with gorgeous photos, fascinating historical tidbits, and practical advice for making the most of your gear, whether it’s a vintage Roland TR-808 or a modern oddity like Erica Synths’ Pērkons. What is the first app you install on a new phone or computer? If I’m buying a new computer, it’ll almost certainly be my music computer, so I’ll be installing Ableton Live straight away. It’s a remarkable piece of music software, with a feature set that still feels staggering compared to when I started making electronic music with an Atari ST 520 that could just about manage MIDI, with no audio at all. Which social media platform do you use the most (if any)? Probably YouTube, if we’re counting it as social media. It’s brilliant having experts in almost any subject area explain ideas, concepts, and methods. I watch a lot of science, maths, chess, and, inevitably, electronic music. I could do with fewer algorithmic clickbait temptations, which is one reason I’m not a heavy user of other social media platforms. Which is the most disappointing gadget you’ve ever owned? Vegetable choppers and cubers seem like a great idea, but they never work properly and never actually save any time or effort. What game do you have the fondest memories of? Elite on the Atari ST was incredible. It’s world-building on a (memory) shoestring when severe technical constraints existed, and the results were truly creative. What is one thing you wish you had created? As a musician, I wish I’d written a song that the whole world knew and loved, and that fans would demand I play at every opportunity — until I got so heartily sick of it that, in the end, I wished I’d never written it. Perhaps this has happened, and all these wishes have come true! What’s the best piece of advice you’ve ever received? From my father (I’m appropriately writing this on Father’s Day in the UK): “Say yes to any opportunity that comes your way — worry about whether you can do it or not later!”  What is your current obsession? Drum machines! Researching for the Beat Gems book has reminded me of the primacy of rhythm to the human musical experience; how drum machines have tapped into this need, and in doing so have transformed musical culture over the last sixty years. It’s utterly fascinating. What do you do when you need to focus? I put on www.rinse.fm/kool, choose a set of banging drum’n’bass rollers, and then I’m very happy (and focused). What do you do when you’re feeling stuck? Remind myself of the infinite number of combinations of ideas. I once wrote an article that demonstrated there were 82 quintillion (82^18) 10-note melodies that can be written with the eight notes of the octave.  What’s the last piece of physical media you bought? The soundtrack on vinyl to a beautiful film called Resynator. It’s about an obscure synth from the early ’80s and a daughter’s quest to learn about her father, who invented it but sadly died while she was a baby. Can’t recommend it enough. What do you think is worth splurging on? A high-quality road bicycle. Compared with cars, bikes are cheap, and you can buy machines not far off the quality professionals use for relatively reasonable sums. The difference between a good bike and a run-of-the-mill one is vast. Cycling in the countryside on a good bike brings me a great deal of joy. What would the tagline for your biopic be? Watch a man type words into a computer. For ages. Then watch him make music on a computer. Also for ages. Then watch him do some normal things involving a house, family, and car. Occasionally he is turned away from boarding a plane to Berlin to go to the launch of his Kickstarter because they changed the rules without him realizing it! Disappointingly, this doesn’t transform the biopic into a Falling Down-type scenario.  What’s the last GIF or meme you used? chineseContent: Oli Freke 是一位音乐家和记者，其作品曾出现在《Sound on Sound》、《The Quietus》和《Mixmag》中。其中包括使用数学来探索西方 12 音阶的旋律潜力以及深入研究效果插件。他甚至写了一本书，追溯了从 1963 年到 1995 年合成器的演变，描绘了从模拟到数字的变化。  他的新项目是 Beat Gems，这是出版商 Bjooks 推出的鼓机咖啡桌视觉历史。与其他 Bjooks 游戏一样，Beat Gems 充满了精美的照片、引人入胜的历史花絮以及充分利用您的装备的实用建议，无论是老式的 Roland TR-808 还是像 Erica Synths 的 Pērkons 这样的现代奇特装备。您在新手机或电脑上安装的第一个应用程序是什么？如果我要购买一台新电脑，它几乎肯定是我的音乐电脑，所以我会立即安装 Ableton Live。这是一款非凡的音乐软件，与我开始使用 Atari ST 520 制作电子音乐时相比，它的功能集仍然让人感到震惊，Atari ST 520 只能管理 MIDI，根本没有音频。您最常使用哪个社交媒体平台（如果有）？如果我们将 YouTube 算作社交媒体的话，可能就是 YouTube。几乎所有学科领域的专家都能解释想法、概念和方法，这真是太棒了。我看了很多科学、数学、国际象棋，当然还有电子音乐。我可以减少算法点击诱饵的诱惑，这也是我不是其他社交媒体平台的重度用户的原因之一。您拥有过的最令人失望的小工具是什么？蔬菜切碎机和切块机似乎是个好主意，但它们从来没有正常工作，也从来没有真正节省任何时间或精力。哪款游戏给你留下了最美好的回忆？雅达利 ST 上的精英
